companies.market: ASML sells lithography machines, the tools that print a chip's circuit pattern with light onto a wafer (a thin silicon disc later cut into chips), plus the service, upgrades and software that keep them running. Its most advanced line uses extreme ultraviolet light (EUV, light of a very short wavelength that can print the finest features). Its newest EUV design, High-NA (optics that gather more light, to print still finer features), has gone mostly to customers' research sites, and the filing says ASML has now released its first full-specification High-NA machine to its first customer. The filing says ASML is currently the world's only maker of EUV machines, and names Canon and Nikon as rivals only in the older deep-ultraviolet machines. Its buyers are chip factories making logic (processors) and memory. In 2025 its logic sales grew, driven by foundries (factories that make chips to other firms' designs) building for AI demand, while its memory sales fell; sales of older machines in China were stronger than it expected. ASML files a 20-F (the annual report foreign companies file with the US regulator) under IFRS, the international accounting rules, so this site's filing reader records no figures for it.
must_be_true: The world keeps building factories for the newest processes (the latest generations of chip-making, which print the smallest features) in logic and memory faster than old ones retire, so demand for EUV machines grows rather than just replacing worn tools.

Chip makers keep shrinking features with lithography rather than with other processes that would need fewer of its machines; the filing names competition from alternative technologies or manufacturing processes only in general terms.
High-NA EUV reaches mass production and customers adopt it on the finest layers, so the next generation is also ASML's alone.
Zeiss and ASML's other single-source suppliers can grow output fast enough that their capacity does not cap its sales for years at a time.
Export rules between the United States, the Netherlands and China do not shut it out of a large block of buyers while a state-backed rival learns to build competing machines.

Customers design their factory processes around its machines and buy its service and upgrades for years after; its service and upgrade sales grew faster than machine sales in 2025, though the filing says part of that came from upgrades to installed EUV machines being counted there instead of as machine sales.

companies.market: Micron makes memory chips: DRAM (the working memory a processor reads and writes constantly), NAND (the storage that keeps data when power is off) and high-bandwidth memory, or HBM (DRAM dies, single chips cut from a silicon wafer, stacked and placed beside an AI chip so they can feed it data very fast). It sells to cloud firms, server makers, phone and PC makers and car makers, and reorganised in 2025 around business units, one of which serves the largest cloud buyers and holds all its HBM sales to data centres. Memory has long been a cyclical, commodity market: its 10-K (the annual report US companies file with their regulator) warns that an oversupplied market pushes prices down, and that heavy investment, including by Chinese state-backed makers, threatens oversupply. This site's filed figures show the swing: Micron made a gross loss (sales below the direct cost of making them) in 2023, and has since swung from losses to a gross margin, the share of sales kept after those costs, among the highest this site has recorded for it. How big the market becomes depends on whether AI keeps memory short, and for how long.
must_be_true: AI keeps raising the amount of memory each unit of computing needs, so memory demand grows faster than the makers can add capacity, cycle after cycle.

Against this unit, this site reads foundry supply as easing: TSMC's capacity is catching up with demand. That undercuts the title's claim for the foundry only if the easing reaches TSMC's own prices and margins, which this site cannot yet see, since TSMC files under international accounting rules this site's filing reader does not read. This site judges that the cost of a unit of computing keeps falling with each chip generation, and that the general-purpose AI chip is being copied from below: every large buyer that designs its own chip, often with Broadcom's help, turns part of NVIDIA's market into a price to negotiate. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part; most goes to buyers as lower prices and better products.

units.kill_shot: NVIDIA keeping both its share of AI chip supply and its gross margin while AMD's chips and the custom chips ship in volume and wafer supply at the newest processes keeps growing fast; or a second foundry making AI chips at the newest process in volume for a major designer.
units.mechanism: Three kinds of firm make AI chips. Designers such as NVIDIA, AMD and Broadcom draw them; a foundry (a factory that makes chips to other firms' designs), above all TSMC, prints them onto wafers (thin discs of silicon, each later cut into many chips); and toolmakers such as ASML build the machines that do the printing. Eliyahu Goldratt, a physicist who studied factories, found that a system runs at the pace of its slowest part. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. So while buyers cannot get enough chips, the designer they most want takes the rent. This site judges that as more chips arrive and the biggest buyers design their own, that rent is exposed, while the foundry and the toolmaker keep theirs for as long as no rival can match what they do.

Eliyahu Goldratt, a physicist who studied factories, found that a system runs at the pace of its slowest part, and David Ricardo, an English economist who studied why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. Oracle set up a programme to sell new shares into the market over time, but had sold none by the end of May 2026. On the neocloud side, CoreWeave's filing says its largest customer, Microsoft, gave it most of its revenue in 2025, that OpenAI and Meta have signed large contracts, that customers commit to take-or-pay contracts (they pay for the capacity whether or not they use it), and that it finances its infrastructure mainly with debt secured on those contracts. Nebius says the long contracts it signed with Microsoft and Meta came with financing terms that let it grow, while most of its customer contracts so far have been short. The hourly rent for NVIDIA's previous-generation flagship chip changed by [fact:h100_rent_yoy] over the past year on this site's latest reading (a minus sign would mark a fall).
units.commoditising: This site judges that an hour on a given GPU is becoming a commodity: the same NVIDIA chips are rented by many firms, Nebius names CoreWeave, Crusoe and Lambda as well as the big clouds among its rivals, and CoreWeave says its customers specify NVIDIA's chips, so the chip, not the cloud, is what they are buying. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part; most goes to buyers as lower prices. On that finding, the rent on each generation of chips falls towards cost as those chips become plentiful. David Teece, an economist who studied why the firm that invents something often fails to keep the returns, called the inputs a product needs to reach its customers complementary assets. This site judges that a neocloud's rack of rented chips is a generic one, which anyone with money, power and a supply of chips can assemble; the scarce inputs behind it belong to others, NVIDIA's chips on one side and the demand of a few big buyers on the other.
units.converts_if: The big clouds turn chip rental into services customers build on, such as their own chips, their own model catalogues and the tools that run AI inside a firm's data, so switching costs hold AI work as they hold older work. For a neocloud: long take-or-pay contracts with buyers who can pay, signed during the shortage, outlast it, and it wins powered sites others cannot get, a cornered resource in Helmer's term (preferential access to something others need). Ronald Coase, an economist who studied why some work is done inside firms rather than bought, and Oliver Williamson, who found that a buyer that depends on an asset built for it can be squeezed by its owner, would expect the biggest buyers to build their own capacity once they can, which is the risk a neocloud's contracts must outlast.
units.kill_shot: Big-cloud margins falling to the neoclouds' level as AI becomes most of what they sell, with customers moving AI work between clouds on price alone; or a neocloud keeping its margin through a year in which GPU rents fall steeply and its largest customer leaves at the end of its contract.
units.mechanism: A cloud rents out computing by the hour or by the contract. The big clouds, often called hyperscalers (Microsoft's Azure, Amazon's AWS, Google Cloud and Oracle), sell AI chips alongside storage, databases and the software businesses already run on them. The neoclouds (newer firms such as CoreWeave, Nebius, Crusoe, Lambda and Fluidstack that rent out mostly NVIDIA's graphics chips, GPUs, and little else) sell the chips almost alone. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. This site judges that a neocloud's margin is that kind of rent, the gap between what a scarce chip rents for and what it costs to buy, power and borrow against, and that it lasts while chips and powered buildings are short; a big cloud's margin rests more on customers whose data and systems already sit inside it.

rival.title: The builders overbuild and rent out the rest

units.stays_scarce: This site judges that what stays scarce is powered, connected data-centre space and, for the big clouds, the customer relationships and the data already stored with them. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier. Scale economies and switching costs apply to the big clouds' existing business today: scale economies (unit costs that fall as volume grows, so a rival must match the volume to match the cost; Google offers its own AI chips, TPUs, beside GPUs) and switching costs (what a customer would lose by moving to a rival, here the work of moving data and systems built around one cloud). This site judges that neither is yet proven for AI work in particular, which is younger and easier to move than the systems firms have run in the cloud for years.
units.title: The big clouds keep a rent from customers who stay; the neoclouds earn the shortage's price on borrowed money

units.case: Open models trail the best closed ones by [fact:open_lag] on this site's latest reading, and on OpenRouter, a service that routes developers' requests to many models, open models took [fact:open_share] of the tokens among its most used models. The price of a given level of capability falls steeply on the estimate of Epoch, a research group that tracks AI, which this site reads as emerging. Against that, the businesses paying for AI, on the card and bill-payment data of Ramp, a firm that handles companies' spending, are concentrated among few labs, while the developers routing through OpenRouter spread their tokens across many more labs. The labs spend far ahead of their revenue: for OpenAI and Anthropic, a year of revenue at the current pace is well below the equity (money investors paid for shares) each has raised, and this site's last reading for xAI, taken before its merger into SpaceX, was also well below. Those revenue figures come mostly from the labs themselves, and investors value the labs at many times that revenue. The labs are buying their way up the stack, into the layers above them that sit closer to users: this site's acquisition ledger counts [fact:lab_deals_now] deals in the past year by which model and computing firms took companies in the layers above, including OpenAI's purchases of consumer apps and of a firm that installs AI inside companies, and Anthropic's of developer tools. Some labs already reach users directly: Google puts its Gemini model into Search and its apps, OpenAI reaches consumers through ChatGPT, its chat app, and Microsoft, which is not a frontier lab on this site's map, holds rights to OpenAI's models for its own products and has a revenue-share agreement with OpenAI. The strongest case against this site's judgement comes from Giovanni Cattani, an investor at Hummingbird Ventures, a venture capital firm, and before that an analyst at Blackstone, a private-investment firm. In an article he published on X, the social network, in early September 2026, titled 'Nobody is talking seriously about AI demand', he argued that the frontier labs' revenue rests on a few open-ended, long tasks, such as AI research, writing software and trading, where buyers always want the best model and will pay the labs' margins; on work with a natural limit, he argued, cheaper models from outside the frontier, firms that run models for others, and small models tuned to one job win instead. On that view the rent holds for as long as the uses of AI keep spreading into open-ended work.
units.commoditising: This site judges that answering a well-understood request, the kind a model from a year before could already handle, is a commodity: many labs and open models do it, and it is priced close to the cost of the chips and power that run it. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part; most goes to buyers as lower prices and better products. Kenneth Arrow, an economist who studied how markets handle knowledge, argued that information is hard to own because copying it is cheap; a model's behaviour can be observed and partly copied by a rival training on its answers.
units.converts_if: Labs turn deployments into switching costs: their coding agents, business tools and staff inside customers become part of how firms work, so moving to a rival means rebuilding, not just repointing. Or a lab owns the place users meet AI, as a chat app with a habit behind it, which Helmer would call branding (a buyer pays more for the same thing because of its name) or network economies (the product grows more useful as more people use it). David Teece, an economist who studied why inventors often fail to keep the returns from what they invent, found that the firm holding the complementary assets (the distribution, sales and systems a product needs to reach buyers) often keeps the profit; Google and Meta already hold theirs, and OpenAI and Anthropic are buying theirs. The rent also lasts, without either, if open-ended uses where only the best model will do keep growing faster than bounded ones, the case Giovanni Cattani makes above. Rules could entrench it too: Sayash Kapoor and Arvind Narayanan, computer scientists at Princeton who study what AI can and cannot do, argued that licensing who may build models, combined with limits on sharing them, would leave only a handful of firms able to build the most capable ones; this site reads that as a route to a regulatory rent (a profit protected by a licence rivals cannot get), which would make the lead last.
units.kill_shot: Labs keeping their price premium and their share of business spending on models that open ones already match, with no growth in deployments or products; or, the other way, business spending spreading across many labs and open models as freely as developers' routed tokens already do.
units.mechanism: The frontier labs, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, xAI and Meta, train the most capable AI models: programs trained on huge amounts of text and data to write, reason and carry out tasks. They sell their use by the token (a fragment of a word) and through products such as chat apps and coding tools. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. Today the scarce input is the best model, and the lab that has it charges for it. This site judges that the rent on a lead is transitional, because open-weight models (whose trained settings, the weights, are published for anyone to run) arrive some months behind, and that it becomes durable only where a lab is woven into how its customers work or owns the place where users meet it.

rival.title: The labs are durable businesses with high margins

units.stays_scarce: This site judges that the newest model at the frontier stays scarce for as long as it leads, and that training one costs so much in chips and money that only a handful of firms attempt it. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier; the one that clearly applies today is scale economies (the cost of training a model is fixed, so a lab with more users spreads it thinner, and a rival must match the users to match the cost). Switching costs (what a customer would lose by moving to a rival) are emerging, not proven: they exist where a lab's tools are built into a firm's systems, but this site cannot yet measure how often firms use several labs at once, so it does not count them in this group's powers.
units.title: A frontier lab's lead earns a rent that open models chase within months; it lasts only where the lab is built into its customers' work

units.case: This site has revenue readings for few of the neolabs. The voice specialist ElevenLabs reports a run-rate (a recent month's revenue scaled up to a year) that rose fast from the end of 2025 to April 2026 and more slowly since, evidence that a specialist off the big labs' path can earn money. For Mistral, a year of revenue at the current pace is well below the equity it has raised, though that gap has narrowed during 2026. The frontier labs' own costs are the hurdle: training at the frontier costs so much that, on this site's reading, even the leading labs' revenue is well below what they have raised. The specialists face a different test: open models trail the best closed ones by only [fact:open_lag], so a new lab's lead in a general model is short-lived, while a specialty in voice, video, robots or science may lie outside what the general labs train for. This site's acquisition ledger counts only purchases of firms in the layers above the models, so it cannot show a neolab being bought, or its leaders hired, by a bigger lab. This site judges which neolabs sit off the big labs' path; it does not measure it.
units.commoditising: This site judges that a general model from a new lab is commoditising fastest of all: it competes with the frontier labs above it and the open-weight labs below it. Kenneth Arrow, an economist who studied how markets handle knowledge, argued that information is hard to own because copying it is cheap; a research idea, once published or seen in a product, spreads to labs with more chips. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part; most goes to buyers.
units.converts_if: A specialist's product becomes the tool a trade works in, so switching costs (what a customer would lose by moving to a rival) hold customers after the general labs catch up; or its data from customers and experiments passes Hagiu and Wright's tests and becomes a cornered resource, Helmer's term for preferential access to something others need. A general neolab converts only if its different route (a new way to train, or a model that learns after it is released) proves both better and hard to copy.
units.kill_shot: A lab founded since 2023 taking the lead on general models and holding it while charging for it; or the specialists' niches being matched by the frontier labs' general models, with the specialists' prices falling to the general labs' level.
units.mechanism: Neolabs are younger AI labs outside the big frontier group, most founded in the last few years and mostly funded by investors before they sell much: Mistral, which publishes the weights (the trained settings) of some of its models, Safe Superintelligence, Thinking Machines Lab, Reflection AI and Periodic Labs among the general and research labs; ElevenLabs, Black Forest Labs and others in voice, images and video; Physical Intelligence and Skild AI in robots. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. For a new lab the scarce input is its researchers and its bet on a route the big labs are not taking. This site judges that where that route leads somewhere the frontier labs are heading anyway, the new lab competes with them for chips and money on worse terms, and its people are worth more to a big lab than its business is to investors.

rival.title: The lead among labs keeps changing hands

units.stays_scarce: This site judges that what stays scarce is the small number of researchers who can lead a frontier training run (the training of the most capable model of its time), and in the specialties, the data and tuning for one kind of work (a voice, a robot's movements, a laboratory's experiments) that general labs have not collected. Andrei Hagiu and Julian Wright, economists who asked when learning from customers' data keeps rivals out, found it does so only when the data is proprietary, keeps its value and improves the product for every customer; a specialty that passes those tests may hold. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier; this site finds no such power proven in the neolabs today.
units.title: A new lab earns a rent only where its specialty lies off the big labs' path; elsewhere its asset is its people

units.case: These readings cover all open models, including Meta's and Mistral's, not only this group's. Open models trail the best closed ones by [fact:open_lag] on this site's latest reading, and on OpenRouter, a service that routes developers' requests to many models, they took [fact:open_share] of the tokens among its most used models, though OpenRouter's users lean towards cheap models and firms that buy from the labs directly never appear there. This site reads the open models' gap to the closed frontier on Epoch's capability index (a score from Epoch, a research group that tracks AI, combining many tests of what a model can do) as unclear: it moves both ways between readings. The labs' finances differ: for MiniMax and Zhipu, a year of revenue at the current pace now exceeds what they raised in their share listings, the only rounds this site records for them; for DeepSeek it is far below.
units.commoditising: The open model is a commodity by design: many hosts serve the same weights and compete on price, so the price of running it falls towards the cost of the chips and power. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part; most goes to buyers as lower prices and better products. This site judges open-weight labs are the clearest case of it in AI: the buyers and the hosts keep most of what the model is worth.
units.converts_if: An open-weight lab's parent earns what the lab gives away: a cloud whose customers come for the free model and stay for the services, which David Teece, an economist who studied why inventors often fail to keep the returns from what they invent, would call owning the complementary assets (the hosting, sales and systems a product needs to reach buyers). Or giving the model away becomes counter-positioning in Helmer's sense, a model a closed lab cannot copy without cutting into its own paid business, with the parent collecting the reward.
units.kill_shot: Closed labs keeping their prices on models that open ones already match, with open models' share of use falling; or an open-weight lab earning a lasting profit on the model itself rather than on hosting, services or a parent.
units.mechanism: An open-weight lab publishes its model's weights, the trained settings that are the model, so anyone can run it on their own chips or rent it from a host. This site's open-weight labs include DeepSeek, Alibaba's Qwen team, Moonshot, MiniMax, Zhipu and StepFun, all of them Chinese; Meta's Llama models are open too, though this site counts Meta among the frontier labs and Mistral among the new labs. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. A model anyone can copy is not scarce, so the lab that publishes it collects little rent on it; this site judges that it earns instead through hosting its own model, selling a better closed version, or serving a parent company or state that wants the model to exist.

rival.title: Labs charge for their lead and let buyers go

units.stays_scarce: This site judges that what stays scarce is the skill to train a model near the frontier on fewer chips, which some of these labs have shown, and the chips themselves, which export rules make harder for Chinese labs to buy. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier; this site finds none proven for the open-weight labs, because a skill that shows up in a published model can be studied and copied.
units.title: Open-weight labs give the model away, so they keep little of its value but cap what the closed labs can charge

units.case: Demand has risen fast on the readings this site holds, all of them company posts or press reports rather than audited figures. Mercor's reported yearly revenue pace, counted before what it pays out to its experts, grew sharply between the start of 2026 and June, and this site reads the expert-data market as emerging; Surge AI was reported to have passed [fact:surge_revenue] of yearly revenue for 2024 without raising outside money. Handshake says that in 2024 the labs wanted qualified experts at scale, that finding and managing them was slow and scattered, and that talent became the bottleneck, and that its long ties with universities spare it the heavy recruiting spending its rivals bear. The labs are pulling the layer closer. Meta bought a minority of Scale AI's shares without votes in June 2025; its filing says it has no significant influence over Scale, but Scale's founder moved to Meta and the two widened their commercial ties. At the time, Scale counted Google, Microsoft and OpenAI among its customers. Scale now says its data underpins work at many of the leading labs, and that it has added large businesses and more government work. Mercor agreed in July 2026 to buy Deeptune, a maker of practice tasks for training, and said the pair would serve companies deploying AI agents (programs that carry out several steps of a task on their own) as well as labs. The leading sellers now offer ordinary companies evaluation (testing an AI system on the firm's own work), post-training (further training of a finished model on narrower material), and help putting systems to work and keeping them running; all of it is on their own pages, not in any filing. Mercor launched an enterprise product in March 2026 that it says maps how a firm's staff do their work, turns that into tests and rules for the firm's agents, and checks their output as they run. Surge AI's enterprise page offers to build tests around a firm's own work, compare models on quality, cost and speed, watch them once live and, where that is not enough, design a training programme and build its data. Scale AI's page says it builds, deploys and runs AI systems for businesses in fields such as energy, insurance and health. Handshake's page says it builds agents inside a client's own systems, lowers what they cost to run and trains models the client owns; in July 2026 it wrote that its tests let a firm find which work can move to cheaper models, among them open-weight ones (models whose trained settings are published so anyone can run them). None of them says how much of its revenue comes from these buyers. Whether expert data is actually short, this site cannot say: nobody publishes its prices or how long buyers wait, so the training-data input carries no tightness reading, and this site's tally of sellers naming labs as customers rises and falls with what sellers choose to disclose.
units.commoditising: This site judges that ordinary labelling, the tagging of pictures and text on which the first data firms were built, is a commodity: many sellers, interchangeable work, and prices set by the pay of the workers. Andrei Hagiu and Julian Wright, economists who asked when learning from customers' data keeps rivals out, found it does so only when the data is proprietary, keeps its value, and improves the product for every customer. For the seller, expert data made to one lab's order fails the first and last of those tests, since the lab owns it and it helps only that lab, and it goes stale as each new model masters what it taught.
units.converts_if: A seller's graded records, pooled across many buyers, become what Helmer calls a cornered resource (preferential access to something others need), such as checked outcomes of expert work that improve every buyer's model; or a seller becomes so built into a lab's training that switching costs (what a customer would lose by moving to a rival) hold it. Coase and Williamson would expect the labs to bring such work inside as it becomes specific to them. Meta's stake in Scale AI is the largest step towards it this site records, but it stops short: the stake carries no votes, and Meta's filing says it gives Meta no significant influence over Scale. The move to ordinary companies is a second route: if tests and graded records built for one firm improve the service for the next, they pass the tests of Hagiu and Wright and would compound; if each job stays made to one client's order, the sellers have swapped a few lab buyers for many consulting clients, paid for their people's time, and the rent stays thin.
units.kill_shot: A seller keeping or widening its margin (what it keeps from each sale after paying its costs) as more sellers enter and the labs hire experts directly, because something it owns, a pool of experts no rival can reach or a record of graded work, grows more valuable with every lab it serves; or a seller earning a lasting margin from ordinary companies on tests and graded records that carry from one client to the next, which would show the rent outlasting the labs' need for people.
units.mechanism: Human-data sellers such as Scale AI, Surge AI, Mercor, Handshake, Turing and Invisible find experts (doctors, lawyers, programmers, scientists), pay them to write questions and answers, grade a model's attempts and set down how they do their work, and sell the result to the AI labs to train on. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. This site judges that the scarce input here is expert time, found quickly and checked well, and that the seller is a broker of it: the work is made to one lab's order and becomes that lab's to keep. Kenneth Arrow, an economist who studied how markets handle knowledge, argued that information is hard to own because copying it is cheap; here the buyer, not the seller, ends up owning it. The leading sellers are now also selling downstream, to ordinary companies rather than labs. Ronald Coase, an economist who studied why some work is done inside firms rather than bought, and Oliver Williamson, an economist who studied contracts and found that whoever has built something useful to only one partner can be squeezed by that partner, explain why the labs pull this layer towards them. This site judges that the move to ordinary companies is the same logic run in reverse: a supplier integrating forward (taking on the next step of the work, closer to the final user) so that it is not at the mercy of a few concentrated buyers.

rival.title: A few large sellers take most of the data market

units.stays_scarce: This site judges that what stays scarce, for now, is the ability to find, vet and pay many experts in a narrow field quickly, and to check their work well enough that a lab trusts it; Handshake's account of its university network and Mercor's stress on its talent network, matching and speed are both claims to that. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier. This site finds none proven here: the benefit of a large expert network is real, but experts can work for several sellers at once and the labs can hire them directly, so the barrier is not yet shown.
units.title: Expert-data sellers broker a skill the labs cannot yet make for themselves; what they sell belongs to the buyer, so their rent lasts only while the labs need people

units.case: This site counts the sellers from one public directory, which in July 2026 showed a small specialist market rather than a crowd; that count says the business exists, not whether it pays. Nobody publishes what environments cost or how long buyers wait, so the post-training input carries no tightness reading. The best sign for the makers is that larger firms are paying to own them. CoreWeave's filing says it bought OpenPipe, a platform for training AI agents by reinforcement learning, in September 2025, and soon after launched, with its Weights & Biases unit, a service that lets customers train this way without managing the machines. In July 2026 Mercor, a seller of expert data, agreed to buy Deeptune, an environment maker, and World Labs, a new lab, bought SceniX, a robotics firm this site files under environments. Buyers that pay to own makers, rather than rent their tasks, are judging that good environments and graders are worth having in-house. Against this unit, the rival view holds that models will set and grade their own practice, and a writer this site follows reports the labs turning from staged practice tasks towards records of real work inside firms; either would leave even expert-graded environments with little to sell.
units.commoditising: This site judges that the practice ground itself, a copied website or a sandbox where code runs, is becoming a commodity: open-source tools and the clouds' own services supply it, and a lab can build one in-house. Andrei Hagiu and Julian Wright, economists who asked when learning from customers' data keeps rivals out, found it does so only when the data is proprietary, keeps its value, and improves the product for every customer. An environment built to one lab's order belongs to that lab, helps only that lab, and goes stale once models master its tasks, since a task every model passes teaches nothing.
units.converts_if: A maker holds graders for a field every lab needs and cannot build, which Helmer calls a cornered resource (preferential access to something others need); or it collects graded outcomes from real work inside firms, which improve with every buyer and go stale slowly. Ronald Coase, an economist who studied why some work is done inside firms rather than bought, and Oliver Williamson, an economist who studied contracts and found that a buyer that depends on an asset built for it can be squeezed by whoever owns it, would expect the labs and compute firms to buy makers whose graders become specific to their training, as the buying so far suggests.
units.kill_shot: Models learning long work whose results are hard to check from practice they set and grade themselves, so the labs stop buying expert-graded environments; or environment makers keeping a lasting margin (what it keeps from each sale after paying its costs) on tasks a machine can already grade.
units.mechanism: Reinforcement learning trains a model by trial and error: it attempts a task, a grader (a program or a person that scores the attempt) marks it, and the model is nudged towards what scored well. An environment is the practice ground: a copy of a website, a codebase, a spreadsheet or a job, with tasks set inside it and a grader attached. Sellers such as Mechanize, Fleet, Halluminate, Matrices, Applied Compute and Plato build them for the labs. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. This site judges that building the practice ground is ordinary software work, so any rent sits in the grader: tasks whose right answer only an expert can judge are scarce, and tasks a machine can check are not.

rival.title: Models make their own practice

units.stays_scarce: This site judges that graders for work whose outcome is hard to judge, such as a legal filing, a clinical call or a long engineering job, stay scarce, together with the experts who can write them. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier; this site finds none proven among environment makers, whose tasks can be rebuilt by a buyer that has seen them.
units.title: Practice tasks for training are made to order for a few labs; they hold value only where the grader checks work that is hard to check

units.case: The clouds and serving firms already sell tuning beside the chips. Google's filing describes Vertex AI as a platform for tuning and deploying custom models and agents from many models, its own and others'; Nebius says its managed service lets companies tune open and custom models; Fireworks says its platform offers tuning, reinforcement learning and testing on top of serving; Baseten says its engineers work inside customers to post-train and serve their models. Compute firms and labs are buying the specialists: CoreWeave's filing records its purchase of OpenPipe, and this site's ledger records Anthropic buying Runhouse in April 2026 and Thinking Machines Lab taking on the Workshop Labs team the same month. Continual learning is young. The highest step this site has seen in production is a pipeline, described by its maker Trajectory, in which a newly trained add-on (an adapter, a thin layer of extra settings) can go live within about an hour; Baseten says it trains a small helper model on the fly from live traffic. Harvey says it worked with Fireworks to post-train its legal model by reinforcement learning in realistic legal work, which this site's ladder of continual learning files as research, not production. Models that keep folding a firm's knowledge into their weights as they work exist only in research. Nobody publishes what post-training costs, so this input carries no tightness reading.
units.commoditising: This site judges that a one-off tuning of an open model on a firm's examples is becoming a commodity: open-source tools such as Unsloth do it for free, the clouds and serving firms bundle it, and each new general model narrows the gain. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part; most goes to buyers as lower prices and better products.
units.converts_if: Continual learning works in production at scale, so a model that has learned a firm's work for months is costly to replace: switching costs in Helmer's sense (what a customer would lose by moving to a rival) for whoever runs it. Ronald Coase, an economist who studied why some work is done inside firms rather than bought, would add that the rent then goes to whoever holds that model, a cloud, a lab, a serving firm or the customer itself, and not necessarily to the firm that did the tuning.
units.kill_shot: Independent tuning firms keeping their margins while the clouds and serving firms bundle tuning with the chips; or, the other way, each new general model wiping out the gains from tuning so firms stop paying for it at all.
units.mechanism: Post-training is everything done to a model after its first, general training, changing its weights (the settings, fixed in training, that hold what the model has learned): tuning it on a firm's own examples, training it by trial and error against graders, and, in its newest form, continual learning, in which the model keeps updating as it is used. Sellers include Thinking Machines Lab, Prime Intellect, Adaptive ML, Predibase, Arcee, Unsloth, Trajectory and Baseten. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. Oliver Williamson, an economist who studied contracts, found that an asset built for one buyer, worth far less anywhere else, ties that buyer to whoever holds it. This site judges that a model tuned to one firm's work is such an asset, but that the tuning itself is a service anyone with chips and open tools (software published for anyone to use and change for free) can offer.

rival.title: General models overtake models built for one field

units.stays_scarce: This site judges that the skill to run reinforcement learning at scale without damaging what the model already knew, and the record of a customer's own work that a continually learning model feeds on, stay scarce. On the tests of Andrei Hagiu and Julian Wright, economists who asked when learning from customers' data keeps rivals out, a customer's record helps only that customer, so it does not compound across customers; but it is specific in Williamson's sense. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier; this site finds none proven among the tuning firms today.
units.title: Tuning a model for one customer is becoming a feature of the clouds and the serving firms; a rent survives only where the tuned model keeps learning inside the customer's work

units.case: This site has no reading of this market's size or prices: it holds no revenue for any seller here, and the training-data input carries no tightness reading. The one move it records is NVIDIA's purchase of Gretel in April 2025, a chip maker taking a data generator in-house. This site judges that the cost of generating falls with the price of running models, which this site reads as easing. A paper this site watches is titled as a study of how generated data can make AI agents (models that carry out tasks by using software tools) forget how to find skills they had learned; this site has read only the title. The best case for a stand-alone seller, in this site's judgement, is privacy: sellers such as Tonic and Mostly AI make made-up copies of real records that banks, hospitals and other regulated firms can use without exposing real people's details, a need a lab's general model does not meet by itself. This site judges that need real but holds no reading of what it earns. No writer this site tracks argues that stand-alone generators win, so this unit names no rival view.
units.commoditising: This site judges that generation itself is a commodity whose cost follows the price of running models down. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part; most goes to buyers as lower prices and better products. David Teece, an economist who studied why the firm that invents something often fails to keep the returns, called the inputs a product needs to reach its customers complementary assets; this site judges that the model and the chips a generator needs are held by the labs and chip makers, not by the generator.
units.converts_if: A generator becomes the kind of copy a regulator accepts in place of real records, such as privacy-safe versions of health or bank data, turning its rent into a regulated one; or its way of checking generated data proves hard to learn, which Helmer calls process power (a way of working that takes rivals years to learn). Ronald Coase, an economist who studied why some work is done inside firms rather than bought, and Oliver Williamson, an economist who studied contracts and found that a buyer that depends on an asset built for it can be squeezed by whoever owns it, would otherwise expect the owners of models and chips to keep generation inside, as NVIDIA did.
units.kill_shot: An independent seller of generated data keeping a lasting margin (what it keeps from each sale after paying its costs) while the labs' own models generate data ever more cheaply; or the labs paying more for generated data than for data from people in the same field.
units.mechanism: Synthetic data is training data that a model or a program generates: made-up records that mimic real ones, worked problems with their answers, rewritten or translated text. Sellers include Datology, Tonic, Mostly AI, Rendered.ai and Synthesis AI; Gretel was one until NVIDIA bought it in 2025. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. Kenneth Arrow, an economist who studied how markets handle knowledge, argued that information is hard to own because copying it is cheap. This site judges that generated data is the plainest case of both: its inputs are a model and computing, which the labs and chip makers already own, so a separate seller has little scarce to charge for, unless it starts from data or a way of checking that others lack.
units.stays_scarce: This site judges that what stays scarce is the check: generated data is only as good as the test of whether it is right. Where a program can check, as when code runs or a proof holds, generated practice is abundant; where it cannot, people must check it, and that scarcity sits with the expert-data sellers and environment makers, not here. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier; this site finds none proven among the generators.
units.title: Generated data is a feature of whoever owns the model and the chips, not a business of its own

units.case: This site holds no reading of licence prices or of how much AI companies pay content owners, and the training-data input carries no tightness reading. It records Cloudflare, which stands between many websites and their visitors, buying Human Native, an AI data marketplace, in January 2026, and its outlook records Cloudflare counting most AI companies' crawlers taking far more pages than they send visitors back. A writer this site follows reports a lab buying an airline's records and data sellers buying those of start-ups that have wound down, which fits the judgement that records of real work, which no one else holds, are what sell. Against this unit, the rival view holds that AI companies will pay for what they read far more widely than for unique archives, and reads Cloudflare's purchase as a step towards a system in which AI developers pay for the content they train on. From the other side, if AI companies can train on public, generated or scraped material instead, even unique archives have little to charge for.
units.commoditising: This site judges that ordinary web text is already a commodity for training: it has been read, copied into many open collections, and cannot be taken back. Kenneth Arrow, an economist who studied how markets handle knowledge, argued that information is hard to own because copying it is cheap. Andrei Hagiu and Julian Wright, economists who asked when data keeps rivals out, found it does so only when it is proprietary, keeps its value and is hard to copy; an archive sold to many labs fails the first test, and old text fails the second once it is in the models.
units.converts_if: Courts or lawmakers settle that training on content needs the owner's permission, turning the owners' rent into a regulated one; or a licensing standard such as RSL becomes what AI crawlers must honour, which could give the brokers network economies in Helmer's sense (each publisher and each AI buyer that joins makes the market more useful to the others). Ronald Coase, an economist who studied why some work is done inside firms rather than bought, would expect the largest buyers to strike direct deals with the largest archives and leave the brokers the long tail.
units.kill_shot: Owners of large, still-growing archives failing to win lasting payments because AI companies train on public, generated or scraped material instead; or ordinary web pages fetching licence prices as high as unique archives do.
units.mechanism: Data licensing is AI companies paying the owners of text, images, audio or records for the right to train on them or to show them in answers. The middlemen this site tracks include TollBit and ProRata, which charge AI companies for reading publishers' pages; Protege, Created by Humans, Defined.ai and Human Native, which broker datasets; and the RSL Collective, which backs a standard way for sites to state their licence terms to AI crawlers (the programs that read websites for AI companies). David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. This site judges that an archive sold once becomes, in effect, part of every model trained on it, while content that keeps coming, such as a forum where people keep writing or a daily news service, can be sold again each year.

rival.title: AI companies pay for what they read

units.stays_scarce: This site judges that archives which are unique, legally clean and still growing stay scarce: a platform's ongoing conversations, a publisher's daily reporting, a firm's records of how its experts work. The power belongs to the owners of those archives, most of whom sit outside this layer; the brokers in it earn a fee. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier; this site finds none proven for the brokers today.
units.title: Licensed content earns a rent only for archives no one else holds that keep growing; the rest is priced near what it costs to copy

units.case: The buying runs one way. CoreWeave's filing says it bought Weights & Biases in 2025, whose tools developers use to build, evaluate, deploy and monitor models and agents; that the unit's results were not material to CoreWeave's; and that the premium it paid over the value of the assets was put down mainly to the team and the expected gains from combining the two. The Humanloop team joined Anthropic in August 2025. OpenAI took on the founders of Context.ai in April 2025, bought Promptfoo, which attacks models to find security flaws, in March 2026, and agreed in December 2025 to buy neptune.ai, which tracks how models train. Fireworks, a serving firm, offers testing on its own platform beside tuning and serving. On the other side, the ledger this site keeps of signs that checking AI's work is sold as a category of its own records [fact:evals_ledger] such events so far. Nobody publishes whether good testing is in short supply, so this input carries no tightness reading.
units.commoditising: This site judges that testing tools, the logging, the scoring against a set of questions and the dashboards, are becoming a commodity: open-source versions exist and the platforms bundle them. Public benchmarks (standard published tests used to compare models) go stale: once a test is published, models are trained towards it. Kenneth Arrow, an economist who studied how markets handle knowledge, argued that information is hard to own because copying it is cheap, and a published test is information.
units.converts_if: Regulators or insurers require an outside tester's sign-off before AI is used in some kinds of work, turning the tester's rent into a regulated one; or one tester's name becomes the mark buyers insist on, which Helmer calls branding. Ronald Coase, an economist who studied why some work is done inside firms rather than bought, and Oliver Williamson, an economist who studied contracts and found that a buyer that depends on an asset built for it can be squeezed by whoever owns it, would otherwise expect the labs and clouds to keep buying testers whose tools become specific to their models, as they have so far.
units.kill_shot: Independent testers growing faster than the labs' and clouds' own testing tools and keeping their margins (what they keep from each sale after paying their costs) as the platforms give testing away.
units.mechanism: Evaluation firms test what a model or an agent can do and watch it once it is running, which the industry calls observability: logging what it did and flagging its mistakes. They include Braintrust, LangSmith (from LangChain), Arize, Galileo, Patronus, Vals AI, Confident AI, Atla, and LMArena, which ranks models by public votes. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. This site judges that testing tools sit close to the models and chips they test, so the firms that sell those can give testing away as a feature; what a buyer cannot get from the seller is a verdict from someone who is not the seller.

rival.title: Checking AI's work becomes a business of its own

units.stays_scarce: This site judges that what stays scarce is a verdict the buyer trusts because the tester does not sell the model: tests for regulated work, for insurers and for buyers choosing between labs, built on private tasks no model has been trained on. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier; the one that would fit here is branding (buyers paying more for the same thing because of who made it), and this site does not find it proven for any tester yet.
units.title: Testing AI is being folded into the labs' and clouds' platforms; an independent tester keeps a rent only where buyers need a judge who is not the seller

units.case: Prices are falling: this site reads the running-models input as easing, from the price of the cheapest flagship model on OpenRouter, a marketplace that routes developers' requests to many models. Open models, which any host can serve, took [fact:open_share] of the tokens among OpenRouter's most used models, though its users lean towards cheap models. Nebius's filing names Fireworks and Together as rivals to its own managed service, which runs all the major open models and lets customers bring their own, and warns that larger rivals may cut prices or bundle. The serving firms describe a way out: Fireworks says nearly all the tokens it serves come from models specialised on customers' own data, and Baseten says its engineers work inside customers to tune and serve their models; both grew revenue sharply and raised large rounds in 2026. Chip and cloud owners are buying serving firms: Nebius agreed in May 2026 to buy Eigen AI and that month took Clarifai's technology and leaders; Nscale agreed in July 2026 to buy Anyscale; Crusoe bought Atero in August 2025; AMD bought Brium in June 2025 and has since bought or taken on other firms that speed up serving; d-Matrix bought Wallaroo.ai in August 2026; and the model labs Mistral and Zhipu agreed in February and June 2026 to buy serving firms. This site holds these firms' reported revenue paces but does not yet publish a reading for the layer.
units.commoditising: This site judges that an answer from a published model is becoming a commodity: the same good from many hosts, with the clouds, the neoclouds (newer cloud firms built to rent out AI chips) and the chip makers all offering it. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part; most goes to buyers as lower prices. David Teece, an economist who studied why the firm that invents something often fails to keep the returns, called the inputs a product needs to reach its customers complementary assets; the chips and powered buildings a serving firm needs are owned mostly by others, which is why their owners can absorb the software on top.
units.converts_if: A host keeps its customers' tuned models, and the loop of data that improves them, so moving to a rival means rebuilding the model: switching costs in Helmer's sense (what a customer would lose by moving to a rival). That route holds only if a tuned model keeps beating each new general model. Ronald Coase, an economist who studied why some work is done inside firms rather than bought, and Oliver Williamson, an economist who studied contracts and found that a buyer that depends on an asset built for it can be squeezed by whoever owns it, would otherwise expect the owners of chips and clouds to keep buying the serving software, as they are.
units.kill_shot: Hosts of the same open model keeping different prices for long, with buyers staying with the dearer one; or serving firms keeping or widening their margins (what they keep from each sale after paying their costs) while chip rents fall and more hosts offer the same models.
units.mechanism: Inference is running a trained model to answer requests. Serving firms such as Fireworks, Baseten, Together, Modal, Replicate, RunPod, DeepInfra and Hyperbolic rent or buy chips, load open-weight models (whose trained settings, the weights, are published) or a customer's own model, and sell the answers by the token (a fragment of a word) or by the hour of chip time. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. This site judges that serving a published model is close to a commodity, since many hosts offer the same model and compete on price towards the cost of chips and power; what a host adds is software that makes each chip answer faster and cheaper, which rivals learn.

rival.title: Models stay different, not interchangeable

units.stays_scarce: This site judges that what stays scarce is the engineering to run each new model fast on each new chip, and, for hosts that tune and run a customer's own model, the position of holding that model. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier. The likeliest here is scale economies (pooling many customers' uneven demand keeps shared chips busy, and a rival must match the volume to match the cost), but the chip and cloud owners can pool as well, so this site does not count it proven.
units.title: Serving a published model is a price-taking business on rented chips; the serving firms are escaping into running each customer's own tuned model, and the chip and cloud owners are buying them

units.case: Developers on OpenRouter spread their tokens (the fragments of words that models read and write, by which use is billed) across many models: this site's first readings of how concentrated its traffic is show no single model dominating, though too few weeks have passed to read a direction, and open models took [fact:open_share] of the tokens among its most used models. Stripe's agreement in August 2026 to buy OpenRouter puts what Stripe calls a leading AI model gateway inside a payments firm, which fits the judgement that its value lies in the bill as much as in the choice. The clouds offer their own catalogues: Google's filing describes a platform with many models, its own, other firms' and open ones. This site cannot measure how much a router saves, because the spread of list prices is set almost entirely by one very expensive model, so its routing gauge carries no reading. The router positions this site records disagree on whether pooling many firms' outcomes makes a router choose better than any one firm can.
units.commoditising: This site judges that picking a model for each request is becoming a commodity: open-source gateways do it, the clouds' catalogues do it, and the labs' own tools do it for their models. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part; most goes to buyers.
units.converts_if: Pooling many firms' checked outcomes lets a router choose better than any firm alone, a network economy in Helmer's sense; or, inside Stripe, the marketplace becomes where AI agents themselves pay for models, so billing and credit create switching costs (what a customer would lose by moving to a rival).
units.kill_shot: Routers charging more for the choice of model itself, and buyers paying it, because choices learned from many firms' outcomes beat what each firm manages alone.
units.mechanism: A router or gateway sits between an app and the models: it sends each request to a model chosen for price, speed or quality, switches when one fails, and keeps one bill. OpenRouter, which the payments company Stripe agreed in August 2026 to buy, sells access to many models through one account; Martian and Not Diamond sell the choice of model; Portkey, Helicone, LiteLLM and TrueFoundry sell a gateway a firm runs itself, LiteLLM's as open source (code published for anyone to use and change for free). David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. This site judges that the routing itself is easy to copy, while a marketplace that many developers and many model sellers both use can hold them the way a payments network does.

rival.title: Routers gain power

units.stays_scarce: This site judges that what stays scarce is the marketplace itself: one account, one bill and one set of terms across many model sellers, and the record of what traffic went where. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier. Network economies (each user makes the product more valuable to the others) would fit a marketplace, but developers use several routers or go straight to the labs, so this site does not count the barrier proven.
units.title: Choosing a model is being given away; a gateway keeps a rent only as the place where developers pay for many models

units.case: The clouds sell agent building as part of their platforms: Microsoft's filing describes Azure AI Foundry as a platform to design, customise and manage AI applications and agents, Google's describes Vertex AI as one for building agents as well as models, and CoreWeave's describes its own agent-building tools. The labs and clouds are also buying the plumbing: Nebius agreed in February 2026 to buy Tavily, which gives agents web search; OpenAI took on the Cirrus Labs team in April 2026 and agreed in June 2026 to buy Ona, which gives agents secure cloud workspaces; Anthropic agreed in May 2026 to buy Stainless, which makes toolkits and servers for connecting models to other software; Meta took in Moltbook in March 2026 and Stilla in September 2026. Platforms are deciding whether to let outside agents in: this site's ledger of big platforms fencing out agents that are not their own records [fact:fences_ledger] such events so far. This site reads agents' ability as easing, meaning the length of task they can finish keeps growing fast; that gauge measures agents, not the economics of their plumbing, for which this site has no reading.
units.commoditising: This site judges that frameworks, sandboxes and simple memory are becoming commodities: most began as open source, the clouds bundle them, and the labs buy the teams that build them. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part; most goes to buyers. David Teece, an economist who studied why the firm that invents something often fails to keep the returns, called the inputs a product needs to reach its customers complementary assets; a generic one, which anyone can supply, earns an ordinary return, not a rent.
units.converts_if: A connector firm becomes the standard way agents are given permission into business software across many firms, which could give it network economies in Helmer's sense (each user makes the product more valuable to the others), or its links into each customer's systems become switching costs. Ronald Coase, an economist who studied why some work is done inside firms rather than bought, would otherwise expect the labs and clouds to keep absorbing this layer, as the buying so far suggests.
units.kill_shot: An open-source framework or sandbox firm earning a lasting margin (what it keeps from each sale after paying its costs) while the labs and clouds give the same thing away; or connector firms losing customers as fast as framework firms once the labs and clouds ship their own connectors.
units.mechanism: An agent is a model that carries out a task by using software tools over minutes or hours. Agent infrastructure is what it needs, much of it open source (code published for anyone to use and change for free): frameworks for wiring model calls together (LangChain, CrewAI, Mastra), sandboxes where it can run code or a browser safely (Daytona, Browserbase and others), memory that lasts between sessions (Letta), and connectors that let it log in to and act in other software (Composio, Arcade, Nango, Merge). David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. Oliver Williamson, an economist who studied contracts, found that an asset built for one buyer, worth far less anywhere else, ties that buyer to whoever holds it. This site judges that frameworks and sandboxes are generic, while connectors that hold a firm's permissions and links into its systems are specific to that firm, and harder to replace.

rival.title: The software that keeps the records gains

units.stays_scarce: This site judges that what stays scarce is the working link into a firm's own software: the permissions, the audit trail and the map of which system holds what. That context helps only the firm it came from, so it does not compound across customers, but it is specific in Williamson's sense. The software that keeps a firm's records can also refuse or charge for outside agents, which is where the rival view places the rent. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier; switching costs (what a customer would lose by moving to a rival) are the likeliest here, but this site does not count them proven for any connector firm yet.
units.title: Agent plumbing is mostly open source that labs and clouds buy or copy; the rent sits with whoever holds the connections into customers' systems

units.case: Palantir's filing describes the route from services to software. It sells platforms that connect a customer's data and operations to large language models (the kind of AI model that reads and writes text) made by other firms; its software engineers working with existing customers run deployments and look for new uses; and it runs short workshops, which it calls bootcamps, that build working tools on a customer's own data within days. It also warns that pilots (trial projects) given at little or no cost may never turn into paying contracts. Much of its revenue comes from existing customers widening their use, and the average revenue from its largest customers rose in 2025 over 2024. No single customer reached the size at which the filing must report it in any year from 2023 to 2025, though governments bring in much of its revenue, and it names large software firms, government contractors and systems integrators (firms that assemble other companies' technology for a client) among its rivals. The labs are buying this layer: this site's record of acquisitions shows OpenAI agreeing to buy Tomoro as it launched the Deployment Company, and the Deployment Company agreeing to buy Northslope, both consultancies that put AI to work in large firms; and Poolside, a lab, buying Fern Labs, a deployment firm. This site's records also hold the Anthropic venture buying Fractional AI and Casper Studios, firms that build AI systems for clients; the record of acquisitions leaves those two out of its count under its written rules, because no single buyer controls the venture. Whether the work pays off is unsettled: in one survey of large firms, most AI pilots built into their systems showed no measurable effect on profit, though another survey, which counts differently, finds many more reaching everyday use.
units.commoditising: This site judges that generic integration, wiring a model to a firm's documents and common business software, is becoming a commodity: the clouds and labs ship connectors (links that let a model read and act in other software) and tools for building agents (AI programs that carry out tasks on their own), and each new model needs less hand-fitting. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part; most goes to buyers. David Teece, an economist who studied why the firm that invents something often fails to keep the returns, called the inputs a product needs to reach its customers complementary assets. This site judges that the deployer owns neither the model nor the customer's records, so on generic work it earns an ordinary services return.
units.converts_if: A deployer's work ends in its own platform, which the customer's operations come to run on, so replacing it means rebuilding the work, not repointing it: switching costs in Helmer's sense. Ronald Coase, an economist who studied why some work is done inside firms rather than bought, and Williamson would add that a lab owning the deployer keeps its model inside that platform, which is why the labs are buying consultancies. The rent stays with services margins if the models learn to fit themselves to a firm's work.
units.kill_shot: Deployment firms keeping or widening their margins while the models need less fitting with each release and the labs give deployment away to win model sales; or, the other way, deployment staff becoming easy to hire while customers still stay with the firm that first fitted their systems.
units.mechanism: Deployment firms send engineers into a customer to connect AI models to its data, systems and daily work. The industry calls them forward-deployed engineers: staff who sit with the customer rather than at head office. This site judges Palantir the largest listed firm doing this work, though Palantir describes itself as selling software platforms. The labs have set up their own deployment arms, among them the OpenAI Deployment Company and a venture Anthropic formed with Blackstone and other investors (reports in this site's records differ on who the others are) to serve companies owned by private-equity firms (investment firms that buy whole companies); and consultancies sell the same work. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. This site judges that the scarce input here is people who understand both the models and the customer's business, and that selling their hours earns a wage-like margin, because each new customer needs more of them. Oliver Williamson, an economist who studied contracts, found that an asset built for one buyer, worth far less anywhere else, ties that buyer to whoever holds it. This site judges that the rent appears only when the deployment leaves behind such an asset: software and a map of the customer's data that its work comes to run on.

rival.title: Engineers who fit AI to each firm are the scarce ingredient

units.stays_scarce: This site judges that what stays scarce is engineers who can turn a firm's messy data and unwritten habits into working systems, and, once that is done, the map of the customer's data and operations that the system runs on. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier. Switching costs (what a customer would lose by moving to a rival) are the likeliest here, and Palantir's expanding customers fit them, but its filing reports expansion, not how many customers leave, so this site does not count the power proven. The rival view holds that these engineers are scarce enough to collect a scarcity rent themselves, not a wage-like margin.
units.title: Fitting AI into a firm earns a services margin that grows with headcount; a rent lasts only where the deployer leaves behind software the customer runs its work on

units.case: Coding agents hold large and fast-rising run-rates (a recent month's revenue scaled up to a year) in this site's records. Cursor's grew sharply between February and June 2026 on press reports citing people close to it; Cognition says its own grew sharply between May and September 2026; and Anthropic said, in announcing a funding round early in 2026, that Claude Code's had grown sharply since the year began. The last two are company figures, not audited ones. This site holds no comparable readings for OpenAI's Codex or for GitHub's tools, though its record of acquisitions shows the teams of small coding-tool firms joining OpenAI's Codex division in 2025 and 2026. The labs and their owners are buying in. SpaceX took an option in April 2026 to buy Cursor for its own shares, and Cursor says the purchase was completed in August. SpaceX's quarterly filing says that alongside the option it agreed to give Cursor computing capacity and to work with it on improving xAI's Grok models and developing new ones jointly; that August Cursor released a Grok model it says the two built together. Cursor says the deal gives it SpaceX's fleet of GPUs (the chips AI runs on) to train stronger models that cost less to run; it had said in late 2025 that its in-house models already wrote a great deal of code. Lovable says it draws on several models, matching each part of a job to the one best suited to it, and tunes open-source models (free code anyone may use and change) of its own. Cognition names large firms, NVIDIA and Citi among them, whose engineering teams use its agent. Google hired away Windsurf's leaders in July 2025 and Cognition agreed to buy the rest of the firm; this site's record of acquisitions also shows OpenAI and Anthropic hiring the teams of smaller coding-tool firms. Microsoft's filing describes GitHub as a platform where developers add AI and agent tools across the whole of building software. Each use costs an app the model's price, which a classic software firm does not pay: ICONIQ, an investment firm, puts the gross margin (sales minus the direct cost of making them, as a share of sales) of the AI products in its survey at [fact:ai_app_margin]. Whether the agents make developers faster is less clear than their revenue suggests: randomised trials (tests that compare groups assigned by chance) by METR, a research group, have not found developers working faster with AI tools, and METR calls the evidence from its newer trial weak.
units.commoditising: This site judges that the agent's wrapper, the editor, the chat window and the loop that lets a model run and test code, is becoming a commodity: several sellers offer much the same, open-source versions exist, and the labs bundle their own with their models. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part; most goes to buyers as lower prices and better products. David Teece, an economist who studied why the firm that invents something often fails to keep the returns, found that the firm holding the scarce inputs a product needs usually keeps the profit; here the lab holds the model, the scarcest input.
units.converts_if: An agent becomes the place a firm's software is planned, reviewed and run, holding its rules, permissions and history, so leaving means rebuilding how its engineers work: switching costs in Helmer's sense. Or its record of developers' corrections trains models of its own good enough to cut what it pays the labs. Ronald Coase, an economist who studied why some work is done inside firms rather than bought, would otherwise expect the owners of models to bring the agents inside, as SpaceX did with Cursor.
units.kill_shot: An independent coding agent keeping its customers and its margin through a year in which the labs cut their own agents' prices and ship better models to everyone at once, with customers not moving to the labs' tools.
