units.mechanism: A coding agent is an AI tool that writes, edits and tests software, from suggesting the next line to carrying out a whole task on its own. The independent sellers include Cognition, Replit, Lovable, Factory and Augment. The labs and their owners sell their own: Anthropic's Claude Code, OpenAI's Codex, and Cursor, made by Anysphere, which SpaceX, the owner of the lab xAI, bought in 2026 and which now works with xAI on its Grok models; and Microsoft sells coding tools through GitHub, a site where developers keep and share code. This site judges that the independent agents mostly run on models bought from the labs, paying by the token (a fragment of a word), though some train models of their own. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. This site judges that the scarce input in a coding agent is the model underneath, which the labs own, so an independent agent keeps a rent only for what it adds: its editor (the program in which developers write and read code), its grip on a firm's code and habits, and its own models where it trains them.

rival.title: Apps keep their margin through what they build around the model

units.stays_scarce: This site judges that what stays scarce is the best coding model at any moment, and, for an agent maker, the record of how developers accept, reject and correct its work, which could train its own models. Andrei Hagiu and Julian Wright, economists who asked when learning from customers' data keeps rivals out, found it does so only when the data is proprietary, keeps its value and improves the product for every customer; a record of accepted code may pass the first and last tests, but goes stale as models improve. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier. Switching costs (what a customer would lose by moving to a rival) are the candidate, but this site judges that a firm can try a rival agent alongside the one it has, and no seller publishes figures on customers leaving, so this site does not count them proven.
units.title: Coding agents are among the fastest-growing AI apps, but the labs sell their own and a lab's owner now holds Cursor; an independent agent's margin is a lease on the labs' models

units.case: Several of these firms report revenue rising fast. Harvey's co-founder said in September 2026 that its annual recurring revenue (what customers have signed up to pay in a year) had grown sharply since January; Legora's chief executive describes the same kind of rise; Decagon told a reporter in August 2026 that its revenue had crossed a large milestone, and a research firm estimates that its run-rate (a recent month's revenue scaled up to a year) rose sharply from the end of 2025; and a research firm estimates that OpenEvidence's run-rate rose sharply between the end of 2025 and July 2026. All of these are company, press or research-firm figures, not audited ones. The apps are building their own assets: Harvey said in September 2026 that it had released its first open-weight model (one whose trained settings are published) tuned for legal work, and that it aims to help law firms build AI they own. OpenEvidence has content partnerships with the New England Journal of Medicine, the Journal of the American Medical Association and the American Medical Association; it gave its research agent free to verified American clinicians in 2025, and it said in March 2026 that most practising American physicians use it every day. Menlo Ventures, a venture-capital firm (one that invests in young companies), found in its survey that start-ups took [fact:startup_app_share] of what American firms spent on AI apps, though the survey leaves out AI built into incumbents' existing software. The labs and platforms are moving into the same trades. Anthropic said early in 2026 that its Cowork product has plugins (add-ons that give its model the tools and instructions for one job) for roles such as sales, legal and finance, and that it had widened its reach into health care; Microsoft's filing describes a cloud business, once called Nuance Healthcare, that sells AI to the health care industry; and this site's record of acquisitions shows OpenAI buying Torch, a health-care technology start-up, in January 2026. The same record shows labs and platforms buying vertical apps: Mistral bought Emmi AI and agreed to buy Pimento, OpenAI bought Crixet, Microsoft bought Fintool and Amazon bought NLX. Where the work is regulated, rules slow everyone: a start-up, UpDoc, said in December 2025 that the Food and Drug Administration had given its diabetes app the first clearance for medical software using large language models that talk to patients, though the agency's own record of the clearance does not describe it that way. Harvey's own test of expert legal work found the best general models finishing few of its tasks end to end in May 2026, a vendor's test not yet repeated by anyone else.
units.commoditising: This site judges that a vertical app that adds only prompts (the written instructions given to a model) and a trade's vocabulary to a general model is becoming a commodity, since each general release learns more trades at once. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part; most goes to buyers as lower prices and better products. Kenneth Arrow, an economist who studied how markets handle knowledge, argued that information is hard to own because copying it is cheap; a clever way of asking a model a legal question is information of that kind.
units.converts_if: A vertical app becomes the system of record for its trade, the software that holds a firm's matters, patients or cases, so switching costs in Helmer's sense hold customers when the labs catch up; or a regulator's approval, or the trade's liability rules, make the app's checked record something a lab cannot simply match, turning its rent into a regulated one. Ronald Coase, an economist who studied why some work is done inside firms rather than bought, would otherwise expect the labs to keep buying the apps whose trades they want.
units.kill_shot: Vertical apps' prices and margins falling each time the labs release a better general model, with customers switching to the labs' own specialist products; or, the other way, a vertical app keeping its customers and prices after a lab ships a rival product for the same trade.
units.mechanism: Vertical AI apps are built for one trade: Harvey and Legora for lawyers, OpenEvidence, Abridge and Ambience for doctors, Hebbia and Rogo for finance, Sierra and Decagon for customer service. They buy models from the labs and wrap them in the forms, checks and records of one kind of work. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. David Teece, an economist who studied why the firm that invents something often fails to keep the returns, found that the profit often goes to whoever holds the complementary assets: the distribution, the trade's trust and the systems a product needs to reach its buyers. This site judges that a vertical app earns a rent only where it holds such assets that a lab cannot copy by training a better general model.

rival.title: Apps that resell the labs' models get squeezed

units.stays_scarce: This site judges that what stays scarce is the place in the trade's daily work (the tool a lawyer drafts in or a doctor's notes are written by), the trade's own records the app is allowed to see, licensed content the trade trusts, such as the medical journals OpenEvidence draws on, and approvals that only a regulator or a licensed professional can give. Andrei Hagiu and Julian Wright, economists who asked when learning from customers' data keeps rivals out, found it does so only when the data is proprietary, keeps its value and improves the product for every customer; much of a trade's data belongs to each client and helps only that client. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier. Switching costs (what a customer would lose by moving to a rival) and branding (buyers paying more because of the name) are the candidates, but these firms are young and publish no figures on customers leaving, so this site counts neither proven.
units.title: A trade's own AI app keeps a rent where it holds the trade's workflow, records and approvals; where it only packages a general model, each lab release takes the margin

units.case: The platforms are putting AI where their users already are. Meta's filing says Meta AI is available across its apps, as a stand-alone app, on its AI glasses and on the web, and that Meta earns substantially all its revenue from advertising. Google's filing says its Gemini model runs across Search and the Gemini app, and warns that as AI enters Search it may earn money differently than it has in the past. OpenAI reaches consumers through ChatGPT directly; its paying subscribers stand at [fact:paid_share] of its weekly users on this site's latest reading, two different counts, so this is not the share of users who pay. The owners of habits are buying small consumer apps: this site's record of acquisitions shows OpenAI buying Roi, Torch, Hiro Finance and NextSlide, Meta buying Manus and Limitless, and Amazon agreeing to buy Bee. Users are getting much of the value: Stanford's Digital Economy Lab estimated what American users would have to be paid to give up generative AI (AI that writes text or makes images on request), and its total rose sharply between the middle of 2025 and early 2026; the survey counts only Americans. This site holds no revenue readings for the companion apps. A wave of personal agents arrived in 2026. Meta says its Muse, launched in September 2026, runs in a sandbox of its own (a separate computer in Meta's cloud, walled off from other users, with its own web browser), books travel, fills in forms and buys things, checks with the user before it sends an email or makes a purchase, and pays through Link, a checkout service built by Stripe; Meta also says Muse is free for most uses with paid plans for more, and does not share users' conversations with Muse, or the data in their Muse workspace, with its ad systems. Instinct, a start-up whose users text it, and whose concierge feature makes phone calls for them, uses its own phone number and computer to carry out tasks, TechCrunch reported when it raised a new round in September 2026 from investors including Sequoia Capital, Benchmark and Coatue, a month after its previous one. Manus, whose makers describe it as a general-purpose agent for research and complex tasks, announced in December 2025 that it was joining Meta. Assistant Benchmark, a site that tests assistants people can text on the same published tasks, ranked Muse first and Instinct second in its tests as of September 2026; the site, created by David Pawlan, says it scored the assistants it tested after real use; it had tested only some of those it lists, so these are one site's results, not a survey of users.
units.commoditising: This site judges that answering an everyday question is a commodity: many free assistants do it well enough, and the price to the user is zero. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part; most goes to users as lower prices and better products. On his finding, the gap between what users would pay and what they are charged is the value they keep. The rival view holds that the labs are durable, high-margin businesses whose customers mostly do not switch, which would leave more of the value with the makers.
units.converts_if: An assistant's memory of each user becomes costly to leave, turning a habit into switching costs in Helmer's sense (what a user would lose by moving to a rival); or assistants learn what people want to buy early enough that advertisers pay more to reach them than in search, turning attention into the kind of rent search earned. It fails to convert if memories become easy to carry from one assistant to another. A third route opens with agents that buy for their users: the agent becomes the place where payment happens, and its owner takes a fee on each purchase, a rent on the sale rather than on attention. That fails to convert if users can move their saved cards, logins and preferences to a rival agent easily, or if shops and payment firms such as Stripe keep the fee.
units.kill_shot: A consumer AI app with no existing platform behind it, such as a personal agent like Instinct, taking a large, paying audience from Meta, Google and ChatGPT and holding it; or consumer AI firms' revenue growing as fast as the value users say they get.
units.mechanism: Consumer AI is the assistants and apps people use for themselves: OpenAI's ChatGPT, Meta AI inside Meta's apps, Google's Gemini in its app and in Search, Perplexity's answer engine, and companion apps such as Character.AI and Replika, which act as a friend or partner. Many people use them free; some pay a subscription, and advertising may pay for the rest. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. This site judges that in consumer AI the scarce input is a user's habit, the app someone opens without thinking, and that it is held by firms that already own people's phones, feeds and searches, plus ChatGPT, which built one of its own. A newer kind of consumer AI, the personal agent (an assistant that carries out tasks for its user, such as booking, shopping, filling in forms and paying, rather than only answering), adds a second question beside the habit: who stands where the user pays.

rival.title: The labs are durable businesses with high margins

units.stays_scarce: This site judges that what stays scarce is the user's attention and habit, the personal history an assistant builds up about each user, and the payment and advertising systems that turn attention into money. David Teece, an economist who studied why the firm that invents something often fails to keep the returns, called those inputs complementary assets; Meta and Google held theirs before AI arrived. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier. Network economies (each user makes the product more useful to the others) and scale economies hold in the platforms' existing businesses, but this site finds none proven for AI assistants themselves, where one user's chat does not make another's better and people use several at once. This site judges that agents which act, not just answer, could move both the habit and the point of payment: if people hand their errands to one agent, the firm running it stands between them and every shop they buy from, and could take a cut of each purchase, as card networks and app stores do, or charge sellers to be chosen. Whether that rent goes to the platforms that already own the habit, such as Meta with Muse and Manus, or to newcomers such as Instinct is open; one tester's early rankings are not evidence of lasting use. Because Meta says Muse keeps users' conversations with it, and the data in their Muse workspace, out of its ad systems, this site judges that, for now, the source suggests any money Muse makes would come from subscriptions or purchases rather than advertising.
units.title: In consumer AI the rent goes to whoever owns the daily habit, and users keep most of the value

units.case: This site holds no revenue or margin readings for any AI rollup; the evidence is structural. The site's automatability census, which screens tasks for whether their shape would let them be handed to software, asks of each trade whether its owner would keep the saving, and answers from how the trade sends its bills. Where the bill counts hours, as in most accounting and audit work, cutting the time cuts the bill and the client keeps the saving, which is why the census calls accounting its false positive. Where the fee is set by something other than the firm's own costs, such as a share of a placed candidate's salary, a commission on a booking or a fixed fee set by the payer, the owner can keep it until the price is next reset. The labs are reaching the same buyers another way: OpenAI has set up the OpenAI Deployment Company, which is buying consultancies that put AI to work in large firms, and Anthropic has formed a venture with Blackstone and other investors (reports in this site's records differ on who the others are) to serve companies that private-equity firms (investment firms that buy whole companies) own. This site's entry for General Catalyst's plan rests on a press report not yet confirmed by a second source.
units.commoditising: This site judges that the AI a rollup uses is bought from the labs and software firms like any other customer's, so it gives no lasting edge over a rival firm that buys the same tools. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part; most goes to buyers. In a trade where clients re-bid their contracts, a saving becomes a lower price once rivals match it. The rival view holds that AI lets one centre see and run many unrelated businesses, an edge that would outlast the tools themselves.
units.converts_if: A rollup turns its running of many firms into a way of working rivals take years to learn, what Helmer calls process power, or grows large enough in one trade and place that its costs per client fall below any single firm's, his scale economies. Both need the saving to outlast the next time clients re-bid, which in trades billed by the hour means moving clients to fixed fees first.
units.kill_shot: AI rollups in trades billed by the hour keeping higher margins for years after buying, without moving clients to fixed fees; or rollups' margins falling back to their trades' ordinary level as rivals that did not merge buy the same AI tools.
units.mechanism: A rollup buys many small firms in one trade, such as accounting, property management or home services, and runs them as one. The groups this site files as AI rollups, among them Thrive Holdings, Long Lake, Crete, Dwelly and Titan, and funds such as General Catalyst that have set money aside to build them, plan to run the firms they buy with AI and keep the saving. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. Ronald Coase, an economist who studied why some work is done inside firms rather than bought, and Oliver Williamson, who studied contracts and found that whoever depends on an asset owned by someone else can be squeezed by its owner, would read a rollup as a bet that owning the customer, the licence and the trust is worth more than selling software to the firm that owns them. This site judges that the bet pays only where the firm's prices do not fall when its costs do.

rival.title: The conglomerate comes back

units.stays_scarce: This site judges that what stays scarce is the customer relationship, a licence or professional's signature where the trade needs one, and prices that are set by something other than the firm's costs. David Teece, an economist who studied why the firm that invents something often fails to keep the returns, called such inputs complementary assets and found that their owners often keep the profit; the rollup buys them rather than building them. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier; this site finds none proven for any AI rollup yet.
units.title: A rollup keeps AI's saving only where the firms it buys are paid for results rather than hours; its asset is the customer, and the AI is bought in

units.case: Use is spreading, but slowly and unevenly. The Census Bureau's survey of American businesses finds [fact:firms_using_ai] of firms using AI in their work. This site sets the normal range for that reading at the pace at which personal computers and online selling spread through firms, and the reading sits inside it. Ramp, a company that handles businesses' card spending and whose customers lean towards technology, puts the median (the middle firm's figure when all are ranked) AI spending per employee at [fact:ramp_spend], against [fact:ramp_spend_year_ago] a year before. Payoffs are hard to find so far: in a survey of executives published in early 2026, most said AI had made no measurable difference to their own firm, and in another survey of large firms most AI pilots (trial projects) built into their systems showed no measurable effect on profit. Studies of single jobs find real but modest gains, as in one study of customer-support staff using an AI assistant. Many workers in the jobs most exposed to AI (those whose tasks AI can most readily do, on researchers' measures) do not yet use it weekly, on the research this site follows. This site's automatability census asks, trade by trade, whether the owner would keep a saving, and finds the answer turns on how the trade sends its bills: by the hour, and the client keeps it; by a fee set elsewhere, and the firm can.
units.commoditising: This site judges that AI itself is becoming a commodity to the adopting firm: the same tools are sold to it and to its rivals, and their price keeps falling. David Teece, an economist who studied why the firm that invents something often fails to keep the returns, found that generic inputs anyone can buy earn only an ordinary return; on his account a firm's advantage from AI lasts only as long as its rivals are slower to adopt it.
units.converts_if: Early adopters rebuild their operations around AI in ways rivals take years to copy, process power in Helmer's sense; or they hold prices that are set by something other than their own costs, such as a share of what the client spends or a fee a regulator sets, so the saving stays with them. Ronald Coase, an economist who studied why some work is done inside firms rather than bought, would add that cheaper checking and contracting could also move work out of firms to AI-run suppliers, handing the saving to whoever runs them.
units.kill_shot: Firms that adopt AI earning higher profits than rivals that do not for years after the tools became widely available, in trades where prices are set by competition; or the share of firms reporting a measurable payoff jumping as use spreads.
units.mechanism: The adopters are the ordinary firms that buy and use AI, from banks and hospitals to shops and law practices. When AI cuts a firm's costs, the saving can go three ways: to the firm as profit, to its customers as lower prices, or to its workers as higher pay. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part and that competition passes most of it on as lower prices. This site judges that the same holds one step down: a firm that adopts AI keeps the saving only until its rivals adopt too, unless its prices are set by something other than its costs. For a layer of buyers, the direction word describes the AI they buy: commoditising means that input is getting cheaper and more alike from seller to seller, so its gains pass to the adopters, unless competition among them passes the gains on again to their own customers.

rival.title: Adoption is not slow; it is hard to see

units.stays_scarce: This site judges that what stays scarce, for the adopter, is the skill to rebuild its work around AI rather than add AI to old work, and its own records of how that work is done. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier; process power, a way of working that takes rivals years to learn, is the one that could fit an early adopter, but this site cannot yet see it in any reading.
units.title: Firms that adopt AI keep its saving only where competition and their pricing let them; so far use is spreading at the pace of past technologies and few report a payoff

units.case: On the consumer side, Stanford's Digital Economy Lab estimated what American users would have to be paid to give up generative AI (AI that writes text or makes images on request), and its total rose sharply between the middle of 2025 and early 2026. On the labour side, the readings are mixed and early. The jobs most exposed to AI are those whose tasks AI can most readily do, on researchers' measures. In those jobs, employment of workers in their early twenties has moved [fact:junior_gap] against older workers since late 2022, against [fact:junior_gap_control] in the least exposed jobs (a minus sign marks the young falling behind), in payroll records that move with anything that treats young and old differently. Revelio Labs, a firm that tracks jobs through online career profiles, finds employment in the most exposed jobs falling behind the least exposed since before ChatGPT's launch, across all ages, with the gap widening in its latest edition; this site reads that as emerging, not a break, and notes that such profiles over-represent office workers. Labour's share of business income changed by [fact:labour_share_yoy] over the latest year (a minus sign marks a fall), which this site also reads as emerging, not a break: the share fell as fast in 2021 to 2023, after the inflation shock, and the latest fall is about as steep as those. The other labour trackers this site follows showed no break it could put down to AI as of the middle of 2026, and a Danish study found chatbots had no measurable effect on earnings or hours in exposed jobs two years in. Jobs in private education and health services and in leisure and hospitality, which stand in for work where the person is part of what is bought, make up [fact:relational_share_now] of American payroll jobs, against [fact:relational_share_year_ago] a year before.
units.commoditising: This site judges that AI's answers are becoming a commodity to the people who use them, free or cheap and offered by many firms, which is why users keep most of their value. Nordhaus's finding is the account of it: competition and copying pass an invention's value to its users as lower prices and better products. For workers, the tasks AI can already do, such as drafting, summarising and routine coding, earn less as the machine's price falls.
units.converts_if: Consumers keep their share only while AI firms compete; a few firms coming to own the assistants people rely on could let them raise prices and take back part of the surplus. Susan Athey and Fiona Scott Morton, economists who study competition, find that when AI is sold by firms with market power, the workers it displaces can lose twice: once when cheap AI cuts their pay, and again when its price later rises. Workers gain a durable share if AI makes their time more valuable than it makes it replaceable, which is what the rise or fall of relational jobs and of pay in exposed jobs would show.
units.kill_shot: AI firms' profits growing as fast as the value users say they get; or labour's share of income falling steeply with employment in exposed jobs, across ages, falling well behind the rest while output rises.
units.mechanism: This layer is people: the workers whose tasks AI can do and the consumers who use it. Consumer surplus is the gap between what people would pay for something and what they are charged, the value they keep. Labour's share of income is the part of what businesses earn that goes to pay rather than profit. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part and that users keep most. Pascual Restrepo, an economist who models how automation changes wages, argues that once machines can do any task, labour's share of income falls towards nothing even as total wages rise. This site judges that for now consumers are Nordhaus's winners, and that workers are paid in wages only as long as their time stays a scarce input. For a layer of people, the direction word describes the split of AI's gains: holding means the split has not yet moved against them, with users keeping most of the value and workers' pay and jobs showing no broad break.

rival.title: Wages follow a jagged path, and the displaced can lose again

units.stays_scarce: This site judges that what stays scarce is work where the person is part of what is bought (care, teaching, hospitality), work someone must answer for, and the skill to direct and check AI across many tasks. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, named the lasting advantages of firms, not people, so none of his powers applies here; the question is only whether workers' time stays scarce enough to be paid for.
units.title: So far users keep most of AI's value; workers' pay and jobs show no broad break, except for the young in the most exposed jobs, though some labour readings are moving
